summary:
Jezero Station is a browser game where kids ages 7 to 12 run a four-person Mars outpost in Jezero Crater for 30 sols. Each sol, players split limited solar power between life support, the greenhouse and the lab, assign crew to tasks, and handle events using the items they saved during a timed scramble before a storm. Crew members can be lost, taking their skills with them, and the game has multiple endings.

It addresses the challenge by making every choice cost something. Shielding takes power and crew time, spacewalks add radiation dose, and Earth’s replies arrive too late to rely on. Radiation events are built from NASA’s DONKI records of real solar flares and coronal mass ejections, and every data-driven element is labeled live, archived or simulated, with sources credited in the game.

It matters because deep space survival is a planning problem under uncertainty, and few young people ever see it that way. Players learn why astronauts must be self-reliant, and why radiation, power and supplies compete, by playing rather than reading.
details:
Jezero Station is a browser game (no download or account) where players run a four-person Mars outpost for 30 sols. Each sol they read what declined overnight, budget limited solar power, assign crew tasks and resolve an event. Before storms a timed scramble decides which items and crew are saved, and those items and crew skills open or close options. Crew can be lost for good, runs end differently, and a random Mission Code reproduces any run.

Real constraints: shielding costs power and crew time, spacewalks add radiation dose that never goes away, dust cuts solar power, and Earth's replies arrive too late. Info buttons explain the science in plain words.

NASA data: radiation events come from NASA DONKI records of real solar flares, coronal mass ejections and particle events, and players can replay a real archived window. Each data element is labeled live, archived or simulated from the actual fetch result, with stored real snapshots as fallback, and a Sources screen credits every dataset. The API key stays server-side.

Tools: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, Motion, GSAP, Web Audio, Vitest, Playwright, Netlify. Difficulty was balanced with thousands of simulated runs by scripted bots.

Creativity: a timed scramble plus a quiet logbook, with paper-cutout art drawn in code. Loss is shown gently and the text is plain.

AI use: code, text and art were produced with AI assistance (DeepSeek via opencode, Claude by Anthropic); sound is generated in code.
